topic: The fall of Nokia, from half the world's phones to selling out to Microsoft
title: Nokia Sold Half the World's Phones. Then It Lost Everything
alt_titles: How Nokia Lost the Smartphone War
The Unbreakable Phone Company That Broke

description:
In 2007, almost half of the phones sold on Earth were Nokias. It was one of the most valuable companies in the world and the pride of an entire country. Just six years later, it sold its phone business to Microsoft.

This is the story of how the company behind the legendary 3310 went from paper mills and rubber boots to dominating the planet, why it didn't see the iPhone as a threat, and how one famous memo described a company standing on a burning platform.

• From a paper mill to the world's phone giant
• The 1100 and the 3310: phones that couldn't die
• A touchscreen prototype years before the iPhone
• The burning platform memo
• Microsoft, Windows Phone and a 7 billion dollar write-off

segments.text: There was a time when, if you had a mobile phone, it was probably a Nokia. In 2007, Nokia sold around four out of every ten phones on the planet. It was one of the most valuable companies in the world, and its phones were so tough that people still make jokes about them breaking the floor when dropped. Six years later, Nokia sold its phone business to Microsoft. And the story of how that happened is one of the fastest falls in business history.

The strangest thing about Nokia is where it came from. In 1865, an engineer called Fredrik Idestam opened a paper mill in southern Finland, next to a river. The town nearby was called Nokia. For more than a century, the company made almost everything except phones. Paper, rubber boots, car tires, electric cables, and later televisions and computers. It was a big, messy industrial group, and by the early nineties it was in serious trouble.

In 1992, a new CEO called Jorma Ollila took control, and he made a radical decision. Nokia would sell or close almost everything else and focus on one thing: mobile phones and telecom networks. At the time, mobile phones were big, expensive and mostly for business people. But Ollila believed that one day, everybody would carry one. It was an enormous bet. And it worked better than anyone could imagine.

Nokia made phones that were simple, cheap, stylish and almost impossible to break. The Nokia 1100 sold around 250 million units, making it one of the best selling phones in history. The 3310 became a legend, with its famous game Snake and a battery that lasted for days. Nokia understood something competitors did not: a phone was not just a tool, it was a personal object. It offered different colors, changeable covers and ringtones.

By 2000, Nokia was worth hundreds of billions of dollars, for a moment the most valuable company in Europe. In Finland, a country of about five million people, Nokia alone represented around a fifth of all exports. It paid a huge share of the country's corporate taxes. Finnish engineers were among the best in the world. Nokia was not just a company. It was a national symbol. And that is exactly what made the fall so painful.

Now here is the twist. Nokia was not a company without ideas. Years before the iPhone, Nokia engineers had built prototypes of phones with touchscreens and internet access. According to former employees, one team even showed a touchscreen phone with an online store for apps. But the managers worried about the cost, and about risking the phones that were already selling so well. The project did not go ahead. Does that remind you of anything? It is exactly the Kodak story, again.

In January 2007, Steve Jobs presented the iPhone. Nokia's reaction, like many in the industry, was calm. The iPhone was expensive, it had a weak battery, it only worked with one carrier in America, and it did not even support fast 3G internet at first. Nokia sold hundreds of millions of phones a year. Apple had never made a phone. What could possibly go wrong? Well, pretty much everything.

The problem was not the hardware. Nokia made excellent hardware. The problem was software. Nokia's phones ran on an operating system called Symbian, which was designed for older phones with buttons. Making apps for it was complicated, and every model was a little different. The iPhone, and a year later Android from Google, offered something new: a simple platform where developers could build apps for millions of users. The war was no longer about phones. It was about ecosystems.

Inside Nokia, many people saw the danger. But the company was huge, with different teams fighting each other, and middle managers afraid to tell their bosses bad news. Researchers who later studied Nokia's fall said the company was full of fear. Leaders were afraid of losing to Apple, and employees were afraid of telling leaders the truth. So Nokia kept promising a new operating system that would fix everything, and kept being late. If you like these stories, subscribe, because we have many more corporate giants to break down.

By 2010, the numbers were terrible. Nokia was still selling a lot of phones, but mostly cheap ones with small profits. Apple and Samsung were taking the expensive smartphones, where the real money was. Nokia's share price had collapsed from its peak. The board decided it needed an outsider, and in September 2010 it appointed the first non Finnish CEO in the company's history: Stephen Elop, a Canadian executive who came from Microsoft.

In February 2011, Elop sent a memo to all employees that became famous. He compared Nokia to a man standing on an oil platform in the sea, which is on fire. The man has two choices: stay and burn, or jump into the freezing water. Elop's message was clear: Nokia was on a burning platform, and it had to jump. Days later, he announced where Nokia was jumping. And it was a very controversial choice.

Nokia would abandon its own systems and use Microsoft's Windows Phone for its smartphones. Many people were shocked. Why not Android, which was growing everywhere? Elop argued that with Android, Nokia would be just one more manufacturer competing on price with dozens of others. With Windows Phone, it could be the main partner. But customers did not want Windows Phone. There were fewer apps, and the phones arrived in a market that had already chosen between Apple and Android.

Sales kept falling. In 2013, Nokia announced it would sell its phone business to Microsoft for around 7 billion dollars. The man who had pushed Nokia to Windows Phone, Stephen Elop, went back to Microsoft with the deal. Many Finns were furious. A quote became famous from that time, widely attributed to a Nokia executive at the press conference: we didn't do anything wrong, but somehow, we lost. Whether or not those exact words were said, they captured the feeling perfectly.

It did not work for Microsoft either. About a year after the purchase, Microsoft wrote off almost the entire value of the deal, more than 7 billion dollars, and cut thousands of jobs. Windows Phone slowly died. The phones that had once been in half the pockets on Earth practically disappeared from the market. In the city of Salo, in Finland, where Nokia phones were made, thousands of people lost their jobs.

But here is something many people do not know: Nokia did not die. The company that remained focused on telecom networks, the antennas and equipment that make mobile internet work. In 2016 it bought the French American company Alcatel Lucent, and today Nokia is one of the few big suppliers of 5G equipment in the world. The brand also returned on phones, made by a separate company under license. It is a smaller Nokia, but it survived.

So what really killed Nokia's phones? Not a lack of engineers, and not a lack of ideas. It was success. When you sell hundreds of millions of phones, every change feels like a risk, and every new idea looks like a threat to what already works. Nokia lost because it was too comfortable to change when change was cheap, and too late when change became inevitable.
Now I want to hear from you. What was your first mobile phone? If it was a Nokia, tell me which model in the comments, and whether you think it would still survive a fall today.

segments.text: In 2007, around four out of every ten phones in the world were Nokias. Nokia engineers had even built touchscreen prototypes years before the iPhone. But managers thought the phones already selling were good enough. Then Apple and Android changed the game from phones to apps. Six years later, Nokia sold its phone business to Microsoft, and Microsoft wrote off almost the entire deal. Success was what killed it. The full story is on the channel.
